items.title: pbzarr
items.text:
pbzarr is a single store for genomic sequencing data that allows for joint computation and storage across data types (tracks), genomic position (position), and samples (column dim). For example, one store can hold coverage and DNase signal for a cohort, together with repeat annotations for stratification.

A store is a Zarr v3 group: a directory, a ZIP file, or a location in cloud object storage. It opens as one xarray Dataset. See Data model for the details.

items.title: Install
items.text:
The Python package needs Python 3.12 or later:

pip install pbzarr

The pbz command-line tool installs into ~/.cargo/bin, on Linux x86_64 or macOS on Apple Silicon:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://github.com/pbzarr/pbzarr/releases/latest/download/pbz-installer.sh | sh

See Install for other systems and options.

items.title: Example
items.text:
PythonCLI 
import pbzarr

ds = pbzarr.open("cohort.pbz")
window = pbzarr.region(ds["depth"], "chr1:100000-101000")
print(window.mean("position").compute())

pbz stat cohort.pbz --track depth -s mean -r chr1:100000-101000

items.title: Upgrading to pbzarr 0.8
items.text: pbzarr 0.8 changes the store format, the command line, the Python API and the Rust crate. This page lists what you must change when you move from 0.7.

items.title: Summary
items.text:
• 0.8 writes and reads format 0.5 only. It cannot open a store made by 0.7 (format 0.4). Import your data again with 0.8.
  • In pbz, the store is now the first argument, and every command takes --track. -o/--output is gone.
  • pbzarr.open now returns one xarray.Dataset. The .pbz accessors are gone. Use the module functions pbzarr.region and pbzarr.reduce_regions.
  • Several flags and keywords have new names. There are no aliases for the old names.
  • New stores use a new default layout: inner chunks of 65,536 positions x 1 column, in shards of 1,024 chunks x 16 columns.
  • BED value columns without data now hold the null (NaN for floats, the type maximum for integers), not 0.

items.title: Stores
items.text:
A 0.7 store has format 0.4. 0.8 refuses it with this error:

This is a format 0.4 store. pbzarr 0.8 reads format 0.5 only. Use pbzarr 0.7, or import the data again.

There is no converter. Import the source files again with 0.8. If you must read old stores, keep pbzarr 0.7 in a separate environment.

Format 0.5 is the draft that format 1.0 will come from. Some rules can still change before 1.0, so a 1.0 reader may not open a 0.5 store.

What changed in the format:

  • In format 0.4, each track was a group with a values array and its own contig and offset arrays.
  • In format 0.5, the store is one zarr group, and each track is an array at the root. The first dimension of a track is position (or bin_N for binned tracks). The contigs are the root arrays contig_id and contig_length. Coordinates are 0-based and half-open.
  • Every import, append and write ends by writing consolidated metadata at the root, so zarr-python and xarray open the store quickly.
  • A format 0.5 store opens as an xarray.Dataset with xr.open_zarr, with no pbzarr code.

items.title: Store and track arguments
items.text:
0.7 0.8 pbz import d4 -o out.pbz --track depth a.d4 b.d4 pbz import d4 out.pbz a.d4 b.d4 --track depth pbz view out.pbz depth pbz view out.pbz --track depth pbz stat out.pbz depth -r regions.bed pbz stat out.pbz --track depth -R regions.bed
  • Import creates the store from the source headers when the path does not exist. When the store exists, import adds the new track. A track name that is already in use is refused.
  • pbz import bed needs --genome only when it creates the store.
  • -v/--verbose is now a global flag. A new global flag -q/--quiet hides the summary line and the progress display.
  • The import summary now goes to stderr, for every import: imported N sources -> PATH (X positions, Y chunks written, Z skipped).

items.title: Renamed flags
items.text: 0.7 0.8 Note --chunk-size N --chunk N Positions per inner chunk. Default 65,536 (was 1,000,000). --shard-size N --shard N The unit changed: it now counts inner chunks per shard, not positions. Default 1,024. --shard-column-size N --shard-columns N Columns per shard. Default 16. -c/--column-dim --dim No short form. --reference (import bam) --fasta -r BED (stat) -R/--regions BED -r now takes one region, CHROM:START-END.

items.title: Removed flags and commands
items.text:
• --column-chunk-size: an inner chunk of a 2D track is now always 1 column wide. Use --codecs for another layout.
  • --dry-run, --in-flight, --scales and --progress (--no-progress stays).
  • pbz scale: multiscale pyramids are no longer made.

items.title: Other changes
items.text:
• pbz view and pbz stat take regions with -r CHROM:START-END (0-based, half-open, repeatable) and -R BED.
  • pbz import bed --emit-schema now takes the BED file as its value: --emit-schema FILE. The schema has a fourth column, fill.
  • --exclude-flags (import bam) also takes hex values and samtools flag names. The default is the same as before.
  • PATH[:LABEL] sources: URLs are no longer split at :. Default labels drop compound extensions (s1.bed.gz gives s1). Paths in a --file-list file are resolved from the folder of that file.
  • pbz view prints an integer null as NaN, and it leaves out rows where every column is null.
  • New commands: pbz append, pbz info and pbz validate. New flag: pbz import --zip.

items.title: Python (pbzarr)
items.text: The package needs Python 3.12 or later.

items.title: Opening stores
items.text:
• pbzarr.open always returns one xarray.Dataset. Each track is a data variable with the name of the track. There is no values variable, and there are no DataTree or collection nodes.
  • The default dask chunks are now about 128 MiB each, made of whole inner chunks. Before, a dask chunk was one stored shard. Use chunks= to set them.
  • open reads .zip stores (read-only).

items.title: Renamed and removed functions
items.text:
0.7 0.8 pbzarr.create_store(path) pbzarr.create(path, reference={"chr1": 248956422, ...}) ds.pbz.region(query, column=...) pbzarr.region(obj, query) (no column=; select columns with xarray) ds.pbz.reduce_regions(intervals, reducer, **kwargs) pbzarr.reduce_regions(obj, intervals, reducer, q=, by=, ddof=, skipna=) ds.pbz.regions(...), dt.pbz.regions(...), dt.pbz.dataset(...) Removed. Use pbzarr.region or pbzarr.reduce_regions. RegionQuery.stop RegionQuery.end

New: pbzarr.write, pbzarr.interval_mask, pbzarr.Reference and pbzarr.__version__.

items.title: Import keywords
items.text:
The changes apply to import_d4, import_bigwig, import_bed and import_bam.

0.7 0.8 column_dim= dim= workers= threads= chunk_size= chunk= shard_size= (positions) shard= (inner chunks per shard) shard_column_size= shard_columns= reference= (import_bam) fasta= column_chunk_size=, in_flight=, scales= Removed column_labels= (import_bam) Removed. Give (path, label) pairs as sources.
  • An import creates the store when it does not exist. You do not need create_store first.
  • import_bed needs genome= only when it creates the store.
  • import_bigwig and import_bed take fill= (a number or "na").

items.title: Import report
items.text: The dict that an import returns has these keys: positions, chunks_written, chunks_skipped, bytes_written and wall_seconds. The other keys (contigs_written, tasks_completed, pieces, the timing keys and others) are gone.

items.title: Region results
items.text:
• The coordinate region_stop is now region_end. region_input_index and region_storage_index are gone.
  • reduce_regions returns rows in input order. Before, they were in storage order.
  • Overlapping intervals are allowed. Before, they were refused.
  • A DataFrame of intervals must have an end column. The stop alias is gone.
  • An option that the reducer does not take raises TypeError.

items.title: Errors
items.text:
• A missing file raises FileNotFoundError.
  • A bad argument, dtype, region or contig raises ValueError.
  • Other failures raise pbzarr.PbzError.
  • Ctrl-C stops an import and raises KeyboardInterrupt.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text:
• Python 3.12 or later (was 3.11).
  • flox is no longer a dependency.
  • New dependencies: pandas and pcodec.
  • Higher minimum versions: zarr>=3.2.1, xarray>=2025.12.0, numpy>=2.4.5, dask>=2026.8.0.

items.title: Rust crate (pbzarr)
items.text:
• PbzStore and Track are replaced by Dataset (open, open_read_only, open_zip, create, create_zip, read_region, validate and more). Measurement::root(&dataset, name) gives the handle of one track.
  • Genome is replaced by Reference. Genome::resolve is now Reference::region.
  • The genome, scale, store and track modules are removed. scale, ScaleConfig and the estimate types are removed.
  • TrackConfig:
  • chunk_size is now chunk.
  • shard_size is now shard, in inner chunks per shard. unsharded() makes a track with no shards.
  • shard_column_size is now shard_columns.
  • column_chunk_size is removed.
  • fill(Fill) sets the fill, and Fill::Na declares the null as the fill value.
  • ImportBuilder::into_track and into_tracks are now into_dataset. options(PipelineOptions) is now config(Config). with_cost_model, with_tap and estimate() are removed.
  • import::Config uses chunk, shard and shard_columns. in_flight_spans, handle_budget and scales are removed.
  • Report has the fields positions, chunks_written, chunks_skipped, bytes_written and wall_seconds.
  • Dtype has I64 and U64.

items.title: Layout
items.text:
0.7 0.8 Inner chunk 1,000,000 positions x 16 columns 65,536 positions x 1 column Shard none 1,024 inner chunks (67,108,864 positions) x 16 columns Codec Blosc zstd level 5, shuffle the same
  • A shard is never larger than the genome or the track width.
  • In our tests with 32 whole-genome samples, the new layout made stores one third smaller (44.4 GB to 29.9 GB) and made 104 files in place of about 6,400.
  • pbzarr.write gives the same layout to new variables whose first dimension is position, unless encoding= sets the layout.

items.title: Fill of BED value columns
items.text:
In 0.7, a BED value column held 0 at positions with no data. In 0.8 it holds the null of its dtype: NaN for floats and the type maximum for integers. The null is the _FillValue of the track, so xarray reads it as NaN, and an integer track then has a float dtype in xarray. A BED value equal to the integer maximum is refused.

Bool columns and BED3 masks still hold false. To get the 0.7 behaviour, use --fill 0 (CLI) or fill=0 (Python).

items.title: Append
items.text: pbz append cannot add columns to a track whose shards hold more than one column, and the new default is 16 columns per shard. To append to a track later, import it with --shard-columns 1.

items.title: Common mistakes
items.text:
Most xarray operations on a store give correct results. A few do not know where one contig ends and the next one starts. This page lists the operations that give a wrong result or an error, and what to do in their place.

The examples use this store:

import pbzarr
import xarray as xr

ds = pbzarr.open("cohort.pbz")
depth = ds["depth"]          # (position, sample)

items.title: Select rows of position directly
items.text:
The mistake: depth[:1000], depth.isel(position=slice(0, 1000)), and depth.sel(position=5) select rows of the flat position axis. The rows have no contig name, and a slice can cross from one contig into the next. The pbzarr functions refuse a slice:

pbzarr.reduce_regions(depth[:1000], ["chr1:0-500"], "mean")
# ValueError: 'position' has 1000 rows but the reference has 320000. This is part
# of the genome. Use the whole array, or region() for one locus.

depth.sel(position=5) gives no error: it reads row 5. Do not use sel on position of a whole-genome array.

Do this: use pbzarr.region for one locus, and pbzarr.reduce_regions for many intervals. Both take the whole track.

locus = pbzarr.region(depth, "chr1:0-1000")
means = pbzarr.reduce_regions(depth, ["chr1:0-500", "chr1:500-1000"], "mean")

On the result of pbzarr.region, sel with labels is correct: locus.sel(position="chr1:500").

items.title: Reorder position
items.text:
The mistake: depth.roll(position=500), depth.sortby(...) along position, or isel(position=order) with all rows keep the full length. The pbzarr functions cannot see the change. They map the rows to the wrong bases, with no error.

Do this: do not reorder position. Reorder the result in its place, for example the rows of pbzarr.reduce_regions.

items.title: Use coarsen or rolling across contigs
items.text:
The mistake: depth.coarsen(position=1000, boundary="trim").mean() and depth.rolling(position=101, center=True).mean() work on the flat axis. The last bin of chr1, and the windows near its end, also use rows from the start of chr2. No warning appears.

Do this: for bins, make one interval for each bin, contig by contig, and use pbzarr.reduce_regions. The last bin of each contig ends at the contig end:

size = 10_000
ref = pbzarr.Reference.from_xarray(depth)
bins = [
    (contig, start, min(start + size, length))
    for contig, length in ref.items()
    for start in range(0, length, size)
]
bin_means = pbzarr.reduce_regions(depth, bins, "mean")

For a window, select one contig with pbzarr.region, then use rolling on it:

smooth_chr1 = pbzarr.region(depth, "chr1").rolling(position=101, center=True).mean()

items.title: Lose the reference coordinate
items.text:
The mistake: most xarray operations keep the reference coordinate. quantile removes it. coarsen keeps its value but removes its index. An array that you make yourself, or that you open with xr.open_zarr, does not have it. The pbzarr functions then refuse the array:

q90 = depth.quantile(0.9, dim="sample")
pbzarr.region(q90, "chr1:0-10")
# ValueError: this object has no pbzarr reference; open it with pbzarr, or pass reference=

Do this: take the reference from the source array, and give it as reference=:

ref = pbzarr.Reference.from_xarray(depth)
locus = pbzarr.region(q90, "chr1:0-10", reference=ref)

items.title: Assign an array from another genome
items.text:
The mistake: two stores can have the same total length with different contigs or a different contig order. Arithmetic between their arrays raises AlignmentError, which is correct. But ds["x"] = other and ds.assign(x=other) give no error. xarray drops the reference of the new array, and the array takes the reference of ds. pbzarr.write then saves the rows in the wrong place.

other = pbzarr.open("other.pbz")["depth"]   # chr2 before chr1, same total length
ds["depth_other"] = other                    # no error, and the rows are wrong

Do this: use xr.merge, which raises AlignmentError when the references are different:

merged = xr.merge([ds, other.to_dataset(name="depth_other")])
# AlignmentError: the objects use different references: ...

Or compare the two references before you assign. The order of the contigs is part of the reference:

same = list(pbzarr.Reference.from_xarray(other).items()) == list(ref.items())

items.title: Select samples before reduce_regions
items.text:
The mistake: this is slow, but correct. pbzarr.reduce_regions reads the store directly when it gets a track as pbzarr.open gave it. After sel(sample=...), isel(sample=...), or transpose, it reads through the Dask graph, which does more work.

Do this: reduce the whole track first, then select samples on the small result:

peaks = ["chr1:10000-20000", "chr2:25000-40000"]
s3 = pbzarr.reduce_regions(depth, peaks, "mean").sel(sample="s3")

For one locus, the order does not matter. pbzarr.region is a plain selection.

items.title: Compute a whole-genome array
items.text:
The mistake: depth.compute(), depth.values, or depth.mean("sample").compute() loads one value for each base into memory. For a human genome, one int32 column is about 12 GB.

Do this: reduce before you compute, for example one value for each region or each sample. To keep a whole-genome result, save it in the store with pbzarr.write. See Save a derived track.

items.title: Data model
items.text:
pbzarr is a single store for genomic sequencing data that allows for joint computation and storage across data types (tracks), genomic position (position), and samples (column dim). For example, a single pbzarr store can be used to represent a cohort of individuals jointly for their quantitative signals (e.g., genomic coverage and DNase), while also storing categorical annotations (e.g., positions of repetitive elements) for stratification in data analysis (panel A). Importantly, this allows for arbitrary computation on or across tracks and their shared dimensions, e.g., an intersection of DNase values across a cohort with repetitive element annotations is a single matrix operation resulting in DNase values stratified by repetitive elements (panel B).

Formally, a pbzarr store is a Zarr v3 group that holds a reference genome defined by contig IDs and contig lengths, and track arrays whose first dimension runs over every base in order, followed by optional labeled dimensions such as sample (panel A, and the format specification). Each track is a Zarr array, which is split into blocks of consecutive positions and samples (chunks) that are compressed and stored independently (panel C). Because a pbzarr store is an ordinary Zarr store, it can be a directory on a file system, a ZIP file, or a location in cloud object storage.

The pbzarr format. (A) A pbzarr store holds a reference genome, defined by contig IDs and contig lengths (blue), and any number of tracks. Tracks share the position axis, which runs over every base in every contig in order (dashed line, contig boundary), and can hold quantitative signals (purple, green) or categorical annotations (red) along a labeled second dimension. (B) Intersecting the DNase track with the repeat track gives DNase values for each sample stratified by repeat class. (C) Each chunk of a track (red outline in A) passes through a Zarr codec pipeline and is stored as one object named by its chunk index (e.g., c/1/0), on a file system or in cloud object storage.

The rest of this page explains each part of a store. After you read it, you can look at print(ds) and name each part.

items.title: What is in a store
items.text:
A store has one reference: a list of contig names and lengths, in order. The store fixes the reference when it is created. Every track covers the whole reference.

A store opens as one xarray Dataset. This is a small store with two contigs and six samples:

import pbzarr

ds = pbzarr.open("cohort.pbz")
print(ds)

<xarray.Dataset> Size: 16MB
Dimensions:        (position: 320000, sample: 6, contig: 2)
Coordinates:
  * sample         (sample) object 48B 's1' 's2' 's3' 's4' 's5' 's6'
    contig_id      (contig) object 16B 'chr1' 'chr2'
    contig_length  (contig) int64 16B 200000 120000
  * reference      <U8 32B 'cca77687'
Dimensions without coordinates: position, contig
Data variables:
    depth          (position, sample) int32 8MB dask.array<chunksize=(320000, 6), meta=np.ndarray>
    mappable       (position) bool 320kB dask.array<chunksize=(320000,), meta=np.ndarray>
    signal         (position, sample) float32 8MB dask.array<chunksize=(320000, 6), meta=np.ndarray>
Indexes:
    reference  ReferenceIndex(2 contigs, cca77687)
Attributes:
    zarr_conventions:  [{'uuid': 'd5bd7bea-0388-4e0a-9844-707c034e9add', 'nam...
    pbz:version:       0.5
Part In the Dataset What it is reference contig_id and contig_length on the contig dimension contig names and lengths, in order position a dimension with no coordinate every base of every contig, one after the other track a data variable whose first dimension is position or bin_N one kind of measurement: here depth, signal, and mappable column axis a dimension such as sample, with a label coordinate of the same name the columns of a 2D track reference a coordinate with no dimension a short digest of the reference, in memory only

The arrays are lazy. pbzarr.open reads the metadata only. pbzarr reads values when you call .compute(), .values, or a function that needs them.

items.title: The reference
items.text:
The reference is the arrays contig_id and contig_length. Their order defines the genome. pbzarr.Reference.from_xarray gives the reference as a mapping of contig name to length:

ref = pbzarr.Reference.from_xarray(ds)
ref["chr1"]          # 200000
list(ref)            # ['chr1', 'chr2']

Each array from pbzarr.open also has a reference coordinate. It has no dimension, so it stays on the result of arithmetic and of most reductions. When you combine arrays from two stores with different references, xarray raises AlignmentError. This stops a silent mix of two genomes. The coordinate is in memory only. The store does not hold it.

items.title: The position axis
items.text:
position holds all contigs, one after the other, in reference order. Its length is the sum of the contig lengths. For the store above, chr1 has 200,000 bases and chr2 has 120,000 bases:

row of position:  0 ........ 199,999 | 200,000 ........ 319,999
base:             chr1:0  chr1:199999 | chr2:0       chr2:119999

The first row of a contig is the sum of the lengths of the contigs before it.

Coordinates are 0-based and half-open, as in BED. chr1:100-200 is 100 bases: the base at 100 is in it, and the base at 200 is not.

position has no label for each base. To read one locus, use pbzarr.region:

locus = pbzarr.region(ds["depth"], "chr2:1000-2000")

<xarray.DataArray 'depth' (position: 1000, sample: 6)> Size: 24kB
dask.array<getitem, shape=(1000, 6), dtype=int32, chunksize=(1000, 6), chunktype=numpy.ndarray>
Coordinates:
  * position       (position) object 8kB 'chr2:1000' 'chr2:1001' ... 'chr2:1998'
  * sample         (sample) object 48B 's1' 's2' 's3' 's4' 's5' 's6'
    region_contig  object 8B 'chr2'
    region_start   int64 8B 1000
    region_end     int64 8B 2000
    pos            (position) int64 8kB 1000 1001 ... 1998 1999
  * reference      <U8 32B 'cca77687'

The locus has labels such as "chr2:1000" on position, so locus.sel(position="chr2:1500") works. Its pos coordinate holds the contig-local positions as numbers. A region string can have these forms:

String Selects "chr1" all of chr1 "chr1:1000" from base 1000 to the end of chr1 "chr1:1000-2000" bases 1000 to 1999 "chr1:1,000-2,000" the same; commas are ignored

The command line uses the same rules for -r. Do not select rows of position directly, for example with ds["depth"][:1000] or isel(position=...). See Common mistakes.

items.title: Tracks
items.text:
A track is one data variable. It has one data type, one fill value, and one set of compression settings. Its first dimension is position (one row for each base) or bin_N (one row for each bin). Values of different kinds go in different tracks. For example, depth, mapping quality, and a mask are three tracks in one store.

A track has one or two dimensions:

  • (position,): one value for each base, for example a mask or a reference signal.
  • (position, sample): one value for each base and each column.

items.title: Column axes
items.text: The second dimension of a track is a column axis. Its name is free: sample, strand, metric, or another name. A column axis has a label array with the same name, and the labels are unique. Tracks that use the same column axis share its labels. In the figure, track_cov and track_dnase share sample, and track_repeats uses repeat.

items.title: Bins
items.text:
A bin_N dimension holds bins of N bases, for example bin_1000. Bins start again at 0 in each contig, so the last bin of a contig can be short. pbzarr.region selects the bins that a region touches.

In this release, pbz view and pbz stat do not read tracks on a bin_N dimension, and pbzarr.reduce_regions leaves them out of its result. Use xarray for these tracks.

items.title: Fill and null
items.text:
The fill of a track is the value at bases that no source covers. A null marks a missing value. Each data type has one null:

Data type Null float32, float64 NaN int8 to int64, uint8 to uint64 the type maximum bool none

Each importer fills gaps in one way:

Importer Value at a gap Change it with d4 0 not possible BAM and CRAM 0 (no reads means depth 0) not possible bigWig null --fill 0, or fill=0 in Python BED value column null --fill 0, or fill=0 in Python BED3 mask, or a bool column false --fill true for a bool column

Use --fill 0 when a gap in the source means 0, as in a bedGraph that leaves out zero regions. Keep the null when a gap means "no value", as in a methylation track.

xarray reads an integer track that has nulls as a float track, with NaN at the nulls. A track of int8, int16, uint8, or uint16 becomes float32. A track of int32, int64, uint32, or uint64 becomes float64. If you need missing values, a float track is often simpler.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Storage layout: chunks, shards, compression, and zip stores.
  • Common mistakes: operations that give wrong numbers with no error.
  • Store format: the rules for tools that read stores without pbzarr.

items.title: Storage layout
items.text: This page explains how a track is cut into chunks and shards, how the chunks are compressed, and when to change the defaults. The defaults are good for most stores. Read this page before you build a large store, or if you plan to add samples later.

items.title: Chunks and shards
items.text:
Zarr cuts each array into chunks and compresses each chunk on its own. A reader decodes whole chunks only. Small chunks make small reads fast, but a genome has billions of bases, so small chunks give a very large number of chunks.

pbzarr solves this with shards. A shard is one stored object that holds many inner chunks and an index of them. A reader can get one inner chunk from a shard and does not read the rest. The file system then has one file for each shard.

The default layout of a track that an import or pbzarr.write makes:

Positions Columns inner chunk 65,536 1 shard 1,024 inner chunks (67,108,864 positions) 16

A shard is never larger than the track. For a short genome or a narrow track, the shard is the size of the track, rounded up to whole inner chunks.

Each inner chunk holds one column. Thus a read of one sample decodes only that sample, also when the shard holds 16 samples.

items.title: Compression
items.text: Each inner chunk is compressed with Blosc, with zstd at level 5 and byte shuffle. Depth and signal data compress well, because neighboring bases often have the same or a near value. A region with no data costs almost nothing. When no source covers a whole chunk, the import does not write the chunk, and a read gives the fill value.

items.title: See the layout of a store
items.text:
pbz info prints the layout of each array:

pbz info cohort.pbz

variables:
  name           role        dtype    dims             shape     chunk    shard     codecs             fill   null  stored   objects
  contig_id      coordinate  string   contig           2         2        -         vlen-utf8          ""     none  20 B     1
  contig_length  coordinate  int64    contig           2         2        -         bytes              0      none  16 B     1
  depth          track       int32    position,sample  320000x6  65536x1  327680x6  bytes,blosc(5)     0      none  1.1 MiB  1
  mappable       track       bool     position         320000    65536    327680    bytes,blosc(5)     0      none  319 B    1
  sample         coordinate  string   sample           6         6        -         vlen-utf8,zstd(0)  ""     none  39 B     1
  signal         track       float32  position,sample  320000x6  65536x1  327680x6  bytes,blosc(5)     "NaN"  none  6.1 MiB  1

chunk is the inner chunk and shard is the shard. stored and objects give the size on disk and the number of stored objects. pbz info --json gives the same data as JSON.

items.title: Change the layout
items.text:
The import commands and functions take three settings:

Command line Python Meaning Default --chunk N chunk=N positions in one inner chunk 65,536 --shard N shard=N inner chunks in one shard, along positions 1,024 --shard-columns N shard_columns=N columns in one shard 16

For example:

PythonCLI 
import pbzarr

pbzarr.import_d4(
    "cohort.pbz", "depth", ["s1.d4", "s2.d4", "s3.d4"], shard_columns=1
)

pbz import d4 cohort.pbz s1.d4 s2.d4 s3.d4 --track depth --shard-columns 1

When to change them:

  • You plan to add samples later. pbz append can grow only a track that has one column in each shard. Import with --shard-columns 1. See Build a cohort store.
  • You read small regions of a very wide track over a network. Each read gets at least one inner chunk for each column. A smaller --chunk makes these reads smaller.
  • Your file system limits the number of files. Larger shards give fewer files. A zip store gives one file.

--codecs (or codecs= in Python) replaces the whole layout with Zarr v3 codec metadata. It is for users who know the Zarr v3 codecs. It cannot be used with the three settings above.

A track keeps its layout. To change the layout of a track, import it again.

items.title: Layout of a written track
items.text:
pbzarr.write gives a new track on position the same layout as an import. The write works one shard at a time. A shard of 16 int32 columns over 67,108,864 positions is 4 GiB in memory, so each Dask worker needs this much memory. For a wide track with less memory, give the layout in encoding=:

import pbzarr

ds = pbzarr.open("cohort.pbz")
callable_ = (ds["depth"] >= 10) & (ds["depth"] <= 60)
ds = pbzarr.write(
    ds,
    {"callable": callable_},
    encoding={"callable": {"chunks": (65_536, 1), "shards": (16_777_216, 4)}},
)

Here a shard holds 16,777,216 positions and 4 columns.

When encoding= gives chunks, shards, or compressors for a track, xarray uses those values in place of the default layout.

items.title: Blocks in memory
items.text: The Dask blocks of an open store are not the chunks on disk. pbzarr.open makes blocks of about 128 MiB. A block holds whole inner chunks and does not cross a shard edge. Thus each Dask task reads whole chunks. Give chunks= to pbzarr.open for other blocks.

items.title: Zip stores
items.text:
A zip store is a whole store in one zip file. It is easy to copy and share, and it is one file on a cluster file system. Make it with --zip, or give a store path that ends in .zip:

pbz import d4 cohort.pbz.zip s1.d4 s2.d4 s3.d4 --track depth

A zip store is written one time. You cannot add tracks or samples to it. pbz view, pbz stat, pbz info, pbz validate, and pbzarr.open read it. pbzarr.write and the Python imports refuse it.

items.title: Zarr, xarray, and Dask
items.text:
pbzarr uses three libraries. Zarr stores the arrays. xarray gives the arrays names and labels. Dask runs the computations in parallel. This page tells you what pbzarr uses from each library, and where to learn more.

You do not need to know these libraries well to use pbzarr. But most work on a store is ordinary xarray and Dask work, so their docs are useful.

items.title: Zarr: the storage
items.text:
Zarr is a format for large arrays. It cuts each array into chunks, compresses each chunk, and keeps each chunk as one object: a file in a directory, an entry in a zip file, or an object in cloud storage. A reader gets only the chunks that it needs.

A pbzarr store is a Zarr v3 group. Each track, coordinate, and label array is one Zarr array in that group. pbzarr adds rules for genomic data: the reference arrays, the position and bin_N dimensions, and the column labels. The store format page gives a map of a store.

Any Zarr v3 tool can read a store. For example, plain xarray opens it with no pbzarr code:

import xarray as xr

ds = xr.open_zarr("cohort.pbz")

Learn more:

  • Zarr documentation
  • Zarr v3 specification
  • Storage guide of zarr-python: local, zip, and cloud stores

items.title: xarray: names and labels
items.text:
xarray adds dimension names, coordinates, and labels to NumPy-like arrays. pbzarr.open returns an xarray.Dataset. Each track is an xarray.DataArray in it.

With xarray, you use dimension names in place of axis numbers:

import pbzarr

ds = pbzarr.open("cohort.pbz")
depth = ds["depth"]

depth.sel(sample="s3")             # one column, by label
depth.mean("sample")               # mean over samples, at each base
(depth >= 10).sum("sample")        # samples with depth 10 or more, at each base
ds["signal"].where(ds["mappable"]) # NaN where the mask is False

Each of these keeps every row of position in place, so the result is correct for the whole genome. pbzarr adds functions only where plain xarray needs to know the genome: pbzarr.region for one locus, pbzarr.reduce_regions for one value per interval, and pbzarr.interval_mask for a mask from intervals.

Learn more:

  • Data structures: Dataset, DataArray, dimensions, and coordinates
  • Indexing and selecting data: sel and isel
  • Computation: arithmetic, reductions, and where

items.title: Dask: lazy and parallel work
items.text:
Dask splits a large array into blocks and runs the work on the blocks in parallel. The arrays from pbzarr.open are Dask arrays. An operation on them makes a plan, but reads no data. The work runs when you ask for values:

over_10 = (depth >= 10).sum("sample")   # a plan; no data is read
result = over_10.compute()              # reads the chunks and runs the plan

The result of .compute() is in memory. Reduce the data before you compute. For example, compute one locus, or one value per region, and not a whole-genome array of many samples.

pbzarr.open gives each track Dask blocks of about 128 MiB, aligned to the chunks on disk. You can give other blocks with chunks=, as in xarray.open_zarr. chunks=None gives arrays that are not Dask arrays: values are read when you index them.

By default, Dask uses threads on one machine. For a cluster, or for a progress dashboard, install dask.distributed (pip install "dask[distributed]") and start a client before you compute:

from dask.distributed import Client

client = Client()   # local cluster; print(client) shows the dashboard address

To save a whole-genome result in the store, use pbzarr.write. It writes the result block by block, so the whole result does not need to fit in memory. See Save a derived track.

Learn more:

  • Dask arrays
  • Parallel computing with Dask in xarray
  • Dask distributed: clusters and the dashboard

items.title: Cookbook
items.text:
Each recipe solves one task. Each recipe has the same parts: the goal, what you need before you start, the steps, and the result.

The recipes use a store cohort.pbz with a depth track over (position, sample). Use your own store and names in their place.

Recipe Task Build a cohort store Import many files as the columns of one track, and add samples later. Depth in regions Get the mean, median, or another statistic for each region and sample. Callable mask Mark the bases with usable depth in each sample, and count them. Compare samples Compare each sample with the cohort, or two samples with each other. Export to bedGraph Write a track or a region as text, from the command line or from Python. Save a derived track Compute a whole-genome result and save it in the store.

items.title: Goal
items.text: Import the per-sample files of a cohort as the columns of one track, with a label for each sample. Add more samples later.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• One file for each sample, all made against the same reference: the same contig names, lengths, and order. This recipe uses d4 files. bigWig, BED, BAM, and CRAM files work in the same way.
  • The pbzarr Python package or the pbz command. See Install.

items.title: 1. Import the files
items.text:
Give the store path, the track name, and the files, each with a column label:

PythonCLI 
import pbzarr

pbzarr.import_d4(
    "cohort.pbz",
    "depth",
    [("s1.d4", "brain"), ("s2.d4", "liver")],
    dim="sample",
    shard_columns=1,
)

A source is a path, or a (path, label) tuple.

pbz import d4 cohort.pbz s1.d4:brain s2.d4:liver --track depth --shard-columns 1

A source is a path, or a path with :LABEL after it.

Without labels, each label is the file name without its extension: s1.d4 gives s1. If one file has a label, all files must have labels.

A shard of one column (shard_columns=1, or --shard-columns 1) lets you add samples to the track later. Without it, a shard holds 16 samples, and pbz append refuses the track. See Storage layout.

items.title: 2. Use a file list for many samples
items.text:
For a large cohort, write the paths and labels in a tab-separated file, one sample on each line. Use it in place of the paths in step 1.

samples.tsv
s1.d4   brain
s2.d4   liver
PythonCLI 
import pbzarr

with open("samples.tsv") as f:
    sources = [tuple(line.rstrip("\n").split("\t")) for line in f if line.strip()]

pbzarr.import_d4("cohort.pbz", "depth", sources, dim="sample", shard_columns=1)

pbz import d4 cohort.pbz --file-list samples.tsv --track depth --shard-columns 1

A relative path in the list starts from the folder of the list file.

items.title: 3. Add samples later
items.text:
Only the command line can add samples:

pbz append d4 cohort.pbz s3.d4:heart --track depth

append adds columns to the track. Other tracks on the sample dimension also get the new column, with their fill value in it.

To start a cohort with one sample, give the dimension name (dim="sample", or --dim sample). Without it, one file makes a track with no column axis, and append cannot grow it.

items.title: 4. Add other tracks
items.text:
An import into an existing store adds a new track. The files must match the reference of the store. A track name can be used one time only:

PythonCLI 
pbzarr.import_bigwig(
    "cohort.pbz", "signal", [("s1.bw", "brain"), ("s2.bw", "liver")], fill=0
)

pbz import bigwig cohort.pbz s1.bw:brain s2.bw:liver --track signal --fill 0

Use a fill of 0 when a gap in a bigWig file means 0. By default a gap is missing (NaN). See Fill and null.

A BED file has no contig lengths. To make a new store from BED files, give a .fai or chromosome-sizes file (genome=, or --genome). An import into an existing store takes the lengths from the store.

items.title: Result
items.text:
PythonCLI 
ds = pbzarr.open("cohort.pbz")
ds["sample"].values      # array(['brain', 'liver', 'heart'], dtype=object)

pbz info cohort.pbz

The output shows the reference, the sample dimension, and one row for each track.

items.title: Goal
items.text: Make a bool track that is True where the depth of a sample is in a usable range, here 10 to 60. Also make a track with the fraction of samples that are callable at each base. Count the callable bases for each sample and each gene.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• A store with a depth track over (position, sample).
  • For the counts in genes: a BED file of genes. See Depth in regions for the file in this example.

items.title: 1. Make the masks
items.text:
import pbzarr

ds = pbzarr.open("cohort.pbz")
depth = ds["depth"]

callable_ = (depth >= 10) & (depth <= 60)                 # (position, sample)
callable_fraction = callable_.mean("sample").astype("float32")  # (position,)

Nothing is computed yet. Both arrays are plans for the whole genome. The name callable_ has an underscore because callable is a Python built-in.

items.title: 2. Save them in the store
items.text:
ds = pbzarr.write(ds, {
    "callable": callable_,
    "callable_fraction": callable_fraction,
})

pbzarr.write computes the masks block by block and saves them as new tracks. It returns the store opened again, so ds["callable"] now reads from the store. A bool mask compresses very well: in the example store, callable takes less than 10 KiB on disk.

items.title: 3. Count callable bases
items.text:
For each sample, over the whole genome:

ds["callable"].sum("position").compute().to_pandas()

sample
s1    316384
s2    317913
s3    317887
s4    317987
s5    313834
s6    317998

For each gene and sample:

import pandas as pd

genes = pd.read_csv(
    "genes.bed", sep="\t", header=None, names=["chrom", "start", "end", "name"]
)
per_gene = pbzarr.reduce_regions(ds["callable"], genes, "sum").compute()
per_gene.to_pandas().set_axis(genes["name"])

sample     s1     s2     s3     s4     s5     s6
name
geneA    9948   9997  10000  10000   9987  10000
geneB   11955  12000  11889  11999  11980  12000
geneC   12937  12998  12999  13000  12984  13000
geneD   14919  14996  15000  15000  11208  15000
geneE    8962   8997   9000   9000   8992   9000

geneD has fewer callable bases in s5, because s5 has a duplication there with depth above 60.

items.title: Variations
items.text:
Limits from the depth of each sample. Samples with different mean depths need different limits. Compute the mean of each sample first, then compare. xarray matches the limits to the sample column:

mean_depth = depth.mean("position").compute()     # one value per sample
callable_relative = (depth >= 0.5 * mean_depth) & (depth <= 2 * mean_depth)

Only inside some regions. pbzarr.interval_mask gives a bool array over position that is True inside the regions:

in_genes = pbzarr.interval_mask(ds, genes)
callable_in_genes = ds["callable"] & in_genes

Export the mask as text.

pbz view cohort.pbz --track callable_fraction -o callable_fraction.bedgraph.gz

pbz view writes runs of equal values as one row, so a mask gives a short file. It prints a bool track as 1 and 0. See Export to bedGraph.

items.title: Result
items.text:
The store has two new tracks:

Track Dimensions Type callable (position, sample) bool callable_fraction (position,) float32

items.title: Goal
items.text: Find regions where one sample differs from the rest of the cohort, for example a deletion or a duplication. Compare two samples base by base.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• A store with a depth track over (position, sample).
  • For the gene table: a BED file of genes. See Depth in regions for the file in this example.

items.title: 1. Correct for the depth of each sample
items.text:
Samples are sequenced to different depths, so compare each sample with its own mean first:

import pandas as pd
import pbzarr

ds = pbzarr.open("cohort.pbz")
depth = ds["depth"]

sample_mean = depth.mean("position").compute()
sample_mean.to_pandas().round(2)

sample
s1    19.88
s2    24.84
s3    29.58
s4    34.77
s5    40.26
s6    29.81

sample_mean has one value for each sample. When you divide by it, xarray matches the values to the sample column.

items.title: 2. Compare each sample with the cohort in each gene
items.text:
Get the mean depth of each gene and sample, divide by the mean of the sample, then divide by the median of the cohort:

genes = pd.read_csv(
    "genes.bed", sep="\t", header=None, names=["chrom", "start", "end", "name"]
)
gene_means = pbzarr.reduce_regions(depth, genes, "mean")
relative = gene_means / sample_mean
ratio = (relative / relative.median("sample")).compute()
ratio.to_pandas().set_axis(genes["name"]).round(2)

sample   s1   s2    s3   s4    s5   s6
name
geneA   1.0  1.0  1.01  1.0  0.99  1.0
geneB   1.0  1.0  0.80  1.0  0.99  1.0
geneC   1.0  1.0  1.01  1.0  0.99  1.0
geneD   1.0  1.0  1.01  1.0  1.25  1.0
geneE   1.0  1.0  1.01  1.0  0.99  1.0

A ratio near 1 is normal. s3 has less depth in geneB, and s5 has more depth in geneD. The ratios are not 0.5 and 2, because the change covers only part of each gene.

items.title: 3. Compare at each base
items.text:
The same steps work at each base. The result is a whole-genome plan, so compute it for one region only, or save it with pbzarr.write:

normalized = depth / sample_mean
ratio_per_base = normalized / normalized.median("sample")

pbzarr.reduce_regions(ratio_per_base, ["chr1:60000-65000"], "mean").compute()

The mean ratio of s3 in chr1:60000-65000 is 0.53: half the depth of the cohort.

items.title: 4. Compare two samples
items.text:
Select two columns and subtract. The result is over position only:

diff = depth.sel(sample="s5") - depth.sel(sample="s1")
pbzarr.region(diff, "chr2:30000-30010").values

depth.sel(sample=...) selects a column by its label, which is correct on a whole-genome track. It is position that must not be selected directly. See Common mistakes.

items.title: Result
items.text:
• ratio: a table of genes by samples. Values far from 1 mark a gain or a loss in one sample.
  • ratio_per_base: the same ratio at each base, as a lazy array over (position, sample). Save it with pbzarr.write to use it again. See Save a derived track.

items.title: Goal
items.text: Get one statistic, such as the mean depth, for each region and each sample. The regions come from a BED file, for example genes or targets.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• A store with a depth track over (position, sample).
  • A BED file of regions. This recipe uses genes.bed, with a name in the fourth column:
genes.bed
chr1    10000   20000   geneA
chr1    58000   70000   geneB
chr1    140000  155000  geneC
chr2    25000   40000   geneD
chr2    90000   99000   geneE

BED coordinates are 0-based and half-open, as in pbzarr.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
PythonCLI

Read the BED file with pandas, and give it to pbzarr.reduce_regions. The table needs the columns chrom, start, and end. Other columns are ignored.

import pandas as pd
import pbzarr

ds = pbzarr.open("cohort.pbz")
genes = pd.read_csv(
    "genes.bed", sep="\t", header=None, names=["chrom", "start", "end", "name"]
)

gene_means = pbzarr.reduce_regions(ds["depth"], genes, "mean").compute()

Row i of the result is row i of the table. Regions can overlap. To show the gene names, use them as the row labels:

gene_means.to_pandas().set_axis(genes["name"]).round(1)

sample    s1    s2    s3    s4    s5    s6
name
geneA   20.0  25.0  30.0  35.0  40.1  30.1
geneB   20.0  25.0  23.7  35.0  40.0  30.1
geneC   17.4  21.7  26.0  30.3  34.7  26.0
geneD   20.0  25.0  30.1  35.0  50.7  30.0
geneE   20.0  25.0  30.0  35.0  40.0  30.0

For a long table with one row for each gene and sample, add the names as a coordinate and use to_dataframe:

table = (
    gene_means.assign_coords(gene=("region", genes["name"]))
    .to_dataframe()
    .reset_index()
)

pbz stat cohort.pbz --track depth -s mean -R genes.bed

#chrom  start   end s1  s2  s3  s4  s5  s6
chr1    10000   20000   19.9962 24.9766 30.0064 34.9678 40.0672 30.0585
chr1    58000   70000   20.0325 24.9805 23.7199 34.9829 39.9717 30.0664
chr1    140000  155000  17.3571 21.6798 25.9696 30.2793 34.6566 26.0133
chr2    25000   40000   20.0264 25.0117 30.0751 34.9839 50.6733 29.9928
chr2    90000   99000   19.9609 24.971  29.9886 34.9624 40.033  30.0061

-s takes mean, min, max, median, or hist. -c s1,s3 selects samples. -r chr1:58000-70000 gives one region on the command line, and you can repeat it. -o means.tsv writes to a file. Without -r or -R, pbz stat gives one row for each contig.

items.title: More statistics in Python
items.text:
The third argument is the statistic: mean, sum, min, max, count, std, var, median, quantile, or summit.

p10_p90 = pbzarr.reduce_regions(ds["depth"], genes, "quantile", q=[0.1, 0.9])
spread = pbzarr.reduce_regions(ds["depth"], genes, "std", ddof=1)

count gives the number of bases that are not null. By default, all statistics skip nulls (NaN in a float track). Give skipna=False to get NaN for a region that has a null.

Give a Dataset to compute the same statistic for many tracks in one call:

both = pbzarr.reduce_regions(ds[["depth", "signal"]], genes, "median")

Regions can also be a list of strings, such as ["chr1:10000-20000", "chr2:25000-40000"], or a list of (contig, start, end) tuples.

items.title: Result
items.text:
gene_means is an xarray.DataArray over (region, sample). Its coordinates region_contig, region_start, and region_end give the region of each row:

<xarray.DataArray 'depth' (region: 5, sample: 6)> Size: 240B
array([[19.9962    , 24.9766    , 30.0064    , 34.9678    , 40.0672    ,
        30.0585    ],
...
Coordinates:
  * sample         (sample) object 48B 's1' 's2' 's3' 's4' 's5' 's6'
    region_contig  (region) object 40B 'chr1' 'chr1' 'chr1' 'chr2' 'chr2'
    region_start   (region) int64 40B 10000 58000 140000 25000 90000
    region_end     (region) int64 40B 20000 70000 155000 40000 99000
  * reference      <U8 32B 'cca77687'

The work reads only the rows of the regions. A call with thousands of regions runs in parallel with Dask. To select samples, select them on the result. See Common mistakes.

items.title: Goal
items.text: Compute a result for the whole genome, such as the fraction of samples with depth 10 or more at each base, and save it in the store as a new track. Then read it again, export it, or use it in other work, with no new computation.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
• A store in a directory. pbzarr.write cannot add to a zip store.
  • Enough disk space for the new track. Most derived tracks compress well.

items.title: 1. Compute the result as a plan
items.text:
import pbzarr

ds = pbzarr.open("cohort.pbz")
over_10 = (ds["depth"] >= 10).mean("sample").astype("float32")

over_10 is lazy. It covers the whole genome on position, and it has the reference coordinate of the store.

items.title: 2. Write it
items.text:
ds = pbzarr.write(ds, {"over_10": over_10})
list(ds.data_vars)       # ['depth', 'mappable', 'over_10', 'signal']

pbzarr.write computes the result one shard at a time and writes each shard. The whole result is never in memory. It returns the store opened again. The Dataset that you gave it does not change, so use the returned Dataset.

The first argument can also be the store path: pbzarr.write("cohort.pbz", {...}).

items.title: 3. Write many tracks in one call
items.text:
ds = pbzarr.write(ds, {
    "depth_mean": ds["depth"].mean("sample").astype("float32"),
    "depth_max": ds["depth"].max("sample"),
})

items.title: 4. Write a value for each sample
items.text:
A variable with no genomic dimension is also accepted, for example one value for each sample:

ds = pbzarr.write(ds, {"mean_depth": ds["depth"].mean("position")})

items.title: Rules
items.text:
pbzarr.write refuses a variable that does not fit the store:

Problem Error The name is already in the store ValueError: 'over_10' already exists in the store Part of position, for example from pbzarr.region ValueError: 'x' has 100 rows on 'position'; the reference has 320000 An array from a store with another reference AlignmentError Sample labels that differ from the store ValueError

The write never changes or removes an existing track. To keep a new version of a result, write it under a new name.

The first dimension of a track must be position or bin_N, and it must cover the whole genome. A new dimension, for example group, needs a label coordinate.

items.title: The layout of a written track
items.text:
A new track on position gets the same chunks, shards, and compression as an import. One shard of 16 int32 columns is 4 GiB in memory. If this is too much for your machine, give smaller shards in encoding=:

ds = pbzarr.write(
    ds,
    {"depth_x2": ds["depth"] * 2},
    encoding={"depth_x2": {"chunks": (65_536, 1), "shards": (16_777_216, 4)}},
)

See Storage layout.

items.title: Result
items.text:
The new track is in the store, and other tools can read it:

pbz info cohort.pbz
pbz view cohort.pbz --track over_10 -r chr1:149990-152010

items.title: Goal
items.text: Write the values of a track as text, for a genome browser or another tool. Write a whole track, some regions, or some samples.

items.title: Before you start
items.text: • A store with a track whose first dimension is position. pbz view does not read tracks on a bin_N dimension.

items.title: 1. Export a whole track
items.text:
pbz view cohort.pbz --track depth -o depth.bedgraph.gz

The output has the columns chrom, start, and end, then one column for each sample. A run of bases with the same values in all columns is one row. A path that ends in .gz writes a BGZF file. Without -o, pbz view writes to stdout.

Use the command line for a whole track. It joins runs of equal values, and it does not hold the track in memory.

items.title: 2. Export some regions or samples
items.text:
PythonCLI

pbzarr.region gives one locus. Select a sample, then convert the locus to pandas:

import pbzarr

ds = pbzarr.open("cohort.pbz")
locus = pbzarr.region(ds["depth"], "chr1:60000-60005").sel(sample="s3")
locus.to_pandas()

position
chr1:60000    12
chr1:60001    13
chr1:60002    18
chr1:60003    14
chr1:60004    16
Name: depth, dtype: int32

For a file with the contig and the contig-local position of each base:

table = locus.to_dataframe().reset_index()
table[["region_contig", "pos", "sample", "depth"]].to_csv(
    "locus.tsv", sep="\t", index=False
)
locus.tsv
region_contig   pos sample  depth
chr1    60000   s3  12
chr1    60001   s3  13
chr1    60002   s3  18
chr1    60003   s3  14
chr1    60004   s3  16

This table has one row for each base, so use it for small regions only. Leave out .sel(sample=...) to get all samples.

pbz view cohort.pbz --track depth -c s3 -r chr1:60000-60005

#chrom  start   end s3
chr1    60000   60001   12
chr1    60001   60002   13
chr1    60002   60003   18
chr1    60003   60004   14
chr1    60004   60005   16
  • -r CHROM:START-END selects one region. Repeat it for more regions. -r chr1 selects all of chr1.
  • -R regions.bed reads the regions from a BED file.
  • -c s1,s3 selects samples, by label.
  • --no-header leaves out the #chrom line.
  • -p 4 prints floats with 4 significant digits. The default is 6.

A null prints as NaN. A row where all columns are null is left out, so gaps in a bigWig import do not fill the file.

items.title: 3. Export one sample for a genome browser
items.text:
A bedGraph file for a browser has one value column and no header:

pbz view cohort.pbz --track depth -c s3 --no-header -o s3.bedgraph

To export a result that you computed in Python, save it in the store with pbzarr.write, then use pbz view. See Save a derived track.

items.title: Result
items.text: A tab-separated text file with 0-based, half-open coordinates, as in BED and bedGraph.

items.title: Try a public store: 1000 Genomes depth
items.text:
This page opens a public store over HTTPS and uses it. You do not download the store. Each step reads only the chunks that it needs.

The store holds the read depth at every base of GRCh38 for the 3,202 samples of the 1000 Genomes Project 30x release.

Property Value URL https://pando-rgw.chpc.utah.edu/vollgerlab/public/pbzarr/30x-1000genomes.pbz Track depth, int32, over (position, sample) Positions 3,217,346,917 (3,366 contigs of the GRCh38 analysis set with decoy and HLA sequences) Samples 3,202 Size 1.5 TiB (41 TB as an array in memory) Source The 30x CRAM files of the New York Genome Center (Byrska-Bishop et al., Cell, 2022)

pbz import bam made the track. The depth counts all reads that are not unmapped, secondary, duplicate, or failed quality control. It counts the overlap of a proper pair one time, and it does not count deletions.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
Install pbzarr. Install aiohttp also, which zarr-python uses to read from an HTTPS URL:

pip install pbzarr aiohttp

items.title: 1. Open the store
items.text:
import pbzarr

URL = "https://pando-rgw.chpc.utah.edu/vollgerlab/public/pbzarr/30x-1000genomes.pbz"
ds = pbzarr.open(URL)
ds

<xarray.Dataset> Size: 41TB
Dimensions:        (position: 3217346917, sample: 3202, contig: 3366)
Coordinates:
  * sample         (sample) StringDType() 51kB 'HG00096' 'HG00097' ... 'NA21144'
    contig_id      (contig) StringDType() 54kB 'chr1' ... 'HLA-DRB1*16:02:01'
    contig_length  (contig) int64 27kB 248956422 242193529 ... 11569 11005
  * reference      <U8 32B '15ba844d'
Dimensions without coordinates: position, contig
Data variables:
    depth          (position, sample) int32 41TB dask.array<chunksize=(65536, 512), meta=np.ndarray>

The open reads the metadata only, which takes about one second. The depth track is a lazy Dask array. No depth values come from the server until you call compute().

Look at the samples and the contigs:

depth = ds["depth"]
depth.sample.values[:4]      # ['HG00096' 'HG00097' 'HG00099' 'HG00100']
ds["contig_id"].values[:3]   # ['chr1' 'chr2' 'chr3']
depth.attrs["description"]

items.title: 2. Read one locus
items.text:
The gene GSTM1 is absent from both chromosomes in many people. Select 40 kb around it, and read three samples:

locus = pbzarr.region(depth, "chr1:109670000-109710000")
three = locus.sel(sample=["HG00096", "HG00100", "HG00103"]).compute()

Positions are 0-based and intervals are half-open. This step reads one inner chunk for each sample, so it takes about one second.

Plot the depth as a mean over 500 bases:

three.rolling(position=500, center=True).mean().plot.line(x="pos", hue="sample")

HG00103 has full depth across the gene, HG00100 has half, and HG00096 has none.

items.title: 3. Compute a statistic for all samples
items.text:
Get the mean depth of GSTM1 and of a control gene, AMPD2, in each of the 3,202 samples:

import pandas as pd

regions = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "chrom": ["chr1", "chr1"],
        "start": [109_687_816, 109_619_836],
        "end": [109_693_745, 109_632_051],
        "name": ["GSTM1", "AMPD2"],
    }
)
means = pbzarr.reduce_regions(depth, regions, "mean").compute()

means is an xarray.DataArray over (region, sample). On a laptop with a home connection, this step took 3 seconds.

Divide the depth of GSTM1 by the depth of the control, and multiply by 2, to estimate the number of copies:

table = means.to_pandas().set_axis(regions["name"]).T
table["copies"] = 2 * table["GSTM1"] / table["AMPD2"]
table.round(2).head()

name     GSTM1  AMPD2  copies
sample
HG00096   1.13  42.34    0.05
HG00097   0.68  39.29    0.03
HG00099   0.70  44.37    0.03
HG00100  18.50  37.38    0.99
HG00101   0.80  42.12    0.04

Count the samples at each copy number:

table["copies"].round().astype(int).value_counts().sort_index()

copies
0    1317
1    1415
2     455
3      15

1,317 of the 3,202 samples have no copy of GSTM1.

Plot the means. The left panel has one point for each sample, with a color for the copy number, rounded to a whole number. The right panel is a histogram of the copies column:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6))
groups = table["copies"].round().astype(int)
for n in sorted(groups.unique()):
    rows = table[groups == n]
    left.scatter(rows["AMPD2"], rows["GSTM1"], s=4, label=str(n))
left.legend(title="GSTM1 copies", loc="lower right", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 0.04), markerscale=3, frameon=False)
left.set_xlabel("mean depth of AMPD2")
left.set_ylabel("mean depth of GSTM1")
right.hist(table["copies"], bins=70)
right.set_xlabel("GSTM1 copies")
right.set_ylabel("samples")

The samples make one line for each copy number. The depth of GSTM1 increases with the depth of the control gene, and the slope of the line gives the number of copies.

items.title: 4. Close the store
items.text: ds.close()

items.title: Python package
items.text:
The Python package needs Python 3.12 or later.

pip install pbzarr

The package has wheels for Linux x86_64 and macOS (Intel and Apple Silicon). The Linux wheel needs glibc 2.28 or later (RHEL and Rocky 8 or later, Ubuntu 20.04 or later, Debian 10 or later).

Check the install:

python -c "import pbzarr; print(pbzarr.__version__)"

items.title: Command-line tool
items.text:
The pbz command is a single binary. To install it, run:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://github.com/pbzarr/pbzarr/releases/latest/download/pbz-installer.sh | sh

The script downloads pbz from the latest release, checks its checksum, and puts it in $CARGO_HOME/bin. If CARGO_HOME is not set, it uses ~/.cargo/bin, the same directory as cargo install. If that directory is not on your PATH, the script adds it to your shell profile. You can change two settings:

Variable Effect Default PBZ_INSTALL_DIR The directory for pbz $CARGO_HOME/bin or ~/.cargo/bin PBZ_NO_MODIFY_PATH Set to 1 to keep the script from changing your shell profile not set 
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://github.com/pbzarr/pbzarr/releases/latest/download/pbz-installer.sh | PBZ_INSTALL_DIR=/opt/bin PBZ_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1 sh

Each release has its own script, which installs that release. To install a specific version, put the version in the URL:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://github.com/pbzarr/pbzarr/releases/download/v0.9.0/pbz-installer.sh | sh

You can also download the binary yourself from the releases page:

System File Linux x86_64 (glibc 2.28 or later) pbz-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz macOS on Apple Silicon pbz-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz

Each file has a .sha256 file next to it. Unpack the file and put pbz on your PATH:

tar -xzf pbz-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz
mv pbz-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/pbz ~/.local/bin/
pbz --version

items.title: Build from source
items.text:
On other systems, build pbz with a Rust toolchain:

cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/pbzarr/pbzarr pbz

items.title: Rust crate
items.text:
Add the core library to a Rust project:

cargo add pbzarr

See Rust for the limits of the crates.io build.

items.text: This page is the --help text of each pbz command. It is generated: run pixi run docs-cli after you change the CLI.

items.title: pbz
items.text:
Per-base Zarr tools

Usage: pbz [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

Commands:
  view      Export one track as bedGraph-like text
  stat      Compute summary statistics for one track
  import    Import data into a PBZ store
  append    Append columns to a track of a format-0.5 PBZ store
  info      Print the reference, dimensions and per-variable layout of a store
  validate  Check a store against the PBZ format rules. Exit code 1 when the store is not valid
  help      Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -v, --verbose...  Increase logging verbosity: -v info, -vv debug, -vvv trace. Warnings and errors always print. `RUST_LOG` overrides this when set
  -q, --quiet       Hide the summary line and the progress display of import and append
  -h, --help        Print help
  -V, --version     Print version

items.title: pbz view
items.text:
Export one track as bedGraph-like text

Usage: pbz view [OPTIONS] <STORE>

Arguments:
  <STORE>  PBZ store to export

Options:
      --track <TRACK>    Track to export. Optional when the store holds exactly one track
  -v, --verbose...       Increase logging verbosity: -v info, -vv debug, -vvv trace. Warnings and errors always print. `RUST_LOG` overrides this when set
  -q, --quiet            Hide the summary line and the progress display of import and append
  -r, --region <REGION>  Region CHROM:START-END, 0-based and half-open as in BED (chr1:0-100 is the first 100 bases). CHROM alone selects the whole contig, also when the name contains ':'. An end past the contig is an error. Repeat for more regions. Without -r or -R, the command reads the whole genome
  -R, --regions <BED>    BED file (plain, gzip, or bgzip) with regions to read after the -r regions. The first three tab-separated columns give CHROM, START, END, 0-based and half-open. Lines that start with #, track, or browser are skipped
  -c, --columns <LABEL>  Column labels of a rank-2 track, comma-separated or repeated. Default: all columns in stored order
  -o, --output <PATH>    Output path. A `.gz` suffix writes BGZF; default is stdout
      --no-header        Do not write the `#chrom start end ...` header line
  -t, --threads <N>      Worker threads for chunk decode and BGZF compression. Default: all cores
  -p, --precision <N>    Significant digits for float values, `%g` style (UCSC bigWig convention) [default: 6]
  -h, --help             Print help

Examples:
  pbz view cohort.pbz --track depth
  pbz view cohort.pbz --track depth -r chr1:0-1000000 -o depth.bedgraph.gz
  pbz view cohort.pbz --track af -c s1,s2 -R targets.bed

Each region is written in order. Rows do not extend across region edges.

The track must have position as its first dimension and at most one other dimension. Tracks on a bin_N dimension are not supported. A null marks a missing value: NaN in a float track, and the _FillValue in an integer track. A float _FillValue must be NaN. view prints a null as NaN and leaves out rows where all columns are null. stat skips nulls.

items.title: pbz stat
items.text:
Compute summary statistics for one track

Usage: pbz stat [OPTIONS] <STORE>

Arguments:
  <STORE>  PBZ store to read

Options:
      --track <TRACK>    Track to compute over. Optional when the store holds exactly one track
  -v, --verbose...       Increase logging verbosity: -v info, -vv debug, -vvv trace. Warnings and errors always print. `RUST_LOG` overrides this when set
  -q, --quiet            Hide the summary line and the progress display of import and append
  -r, --region <REGION>  Region CHROM:START-END, 0-based and half-open as in BED (chr1:0-100 is the first 100 bases). CHROM alone selects the whole contig, also when the name contains ':'. An end past the contig is an error. Repeat for more regions. Without -r or -R, the command reads the whole genome
  -R, --regions <BED>    BED file (plain, gzip, or bgzip) with regions to read after the -r regions. The first three tab-separated columns give CHROM, START, END, 0-based and half-open. Lines that start with #, track, or browser are skipped
  -s, --stat <STAT>      Statistic to compute [default: mean] [possible values: mean, min, max, median, hist]
  -c, --columns <LABEL>  Column labels of a rank-2 track, comma-separated or repeated. Default: all columns in stored order
  -o, --output <PATH>    Output path. A `.gz` suffix writes BGZF; default is stdout
      --no-header        Do not write the header line
  -t, --threads <N>      Worker threads for chunk decode and stat batches. Default: all cores
  -p, --precision <N>    Significant digits for float values, `%g` style [default: 6]
  -h, --help             Print help

The track must have position as its first dimension and at most one other dimension. Tracks on a bin_N dimension are not supported. A null marks a missing value: NaN in a float track, and the _FillValue in an integer track. A float _FillValue must be NaN. view prints a null as NaN and leaves out rows where all columns are null. stat skips nulls.

items.title: pbz import bed
items.text:
Import from tabix-indexed BED files

Usage: pbz import bed [OPTIONS] [STORE] [PATH[:LABEL]]...

Arguments:
  [STORE]            PBZ store to write. Import creates it when the path does not exist, and adds the track(s) to it when it exists
  [PATH[:LABEL]]...  Input files, optionally suffixed with `:LABEL`. The default label is the file name without its format extension (`s1.bed.gz` gives `s1`)

Options:
  -t, --threads <THREADS>    Worker threads for decode and write [default: 4]
  -v, --verbose...           Increase logging verbosity: -v info, -vv debug, -vvv trace. Warnings and errors always print. `RUST_LOG` overrides this when set
      --decode-chunks <N>    Position chunks each reader decodes per read pass. Default: auto (up to 4M positions, fewer when that leaves workers short of pieces)
  -q, --quiet                Hide the summary line and the progress display of import and append
      --no-progress          Hide the progress display
      --chunk <N>            Positions per inner chunk. A 2D track has one column per inner chunk. Default: 65,536
      --shard <N>            Inner chunks per shard along positions, so a shard holds chunk x N positions. A shard is capped at the genome length, rounded up to whole chunks. Default: 1,024
      --shard-columns <N>    Columns per shard of a 2D track. A shard is capped at the track width. Default: 16. Give 1 to make a track that pbz append can grow
      --dim <NAME>           Name of the second dimension of a 2D track. A single source with --dim still makes a 2D track. Default: `sample` for several d4, bigWig or BAM sources. BED import has no default: it needs --dim whenever the output is 2D (several sources, or several BED columns in one track)
      --codecs <JSON|@FILE>  Zarr v3 codec metadata for the created track arrays: a `codecs` JSON array, or a `{"chunk_grid": ..., "codecs": [...]}` fragment. Pass `@path` to read the JSON from a file. Replaces the default Blosc(zstd-5, byte shuffle) pipeline and the whole chunk and shard layout; express sharding as a `sharding_indexed` codec and the outer grid as `chunk_grid`. Without `chunk_grid`, the outer grid is 65,536 positions by 16 columns, capped at the track width
      --zip                  Write a new single-file zip store. A STORE path that ends in `.zip` also does this. The path must not exist
  -f, --file-list <PATH>     Tab-delimited source list with PATH or PATH<TAB>LABEL records. Relative paths start from the directory of the list file
      --genome <GENOME>      FAI or chromosome-sizes file with the contig lengths. It is needed only when the store does not exist; an existing store gives its own
      --field <FIELDS>       BED header column to import (requires a `#`-prefixed header). Repeating selects several BED columns; omit to import all BED value columns
      --track <TRACK>        Output track name. Required for BED3, headerless BED4, and when several BED columns from one source form one wide track
      --dtype <DTYPE>        Value dtype for headerless BED4 input (inferred when omitted) [possible values: bool, uint8, uint16, uint32, uint64, int8, int16, int32, int64, float32, float64]
      --schema <PATH>        TSV schema mapping BED columns to target tracks. Unique target names create one track per BED column; repeated one-target rows create a single BED-column-axis track. A BED column is a header name or 1-based column index. A row can also give the dtype and the fill of its track
      --emit-schema <BED>    Print a schema TSV for this BED file (BED column, target track, inferred dtype, fill) to stdout and exit without importing. Edit it and feed it back via --schema
      --fill <VALUE|na>      Value of bases that no interval covers, for BED value columns: a number, true or false for a bool column, or na. na is the null of the dtype: NaN for a float, the type maximum for an integer. Default: na, and false for a bool column. BED3 masks always hold false
      --infer-rows <N|all>   Records sampled for dtype inference (default 1000), or `all`. A sample infers conservative classes (bool/int32/float32); `all` (or a file smaller than the sample) scans exhaustively and min-widths (uint8, int16, ...)
  -h, --help                 Print help

Examples:
  pbz import bed cohort.pbz s1.bed.gz s2.bed.gz --genome genome.fai --track depth --dim sample
  pbz import bed mask.pbz regions.bed.gz --genome genome.fai --track callable
  pbz import bed --emit-schema wide.bed.gz > schema.tsv
  pbz import bed stats.pbz wide.bed.gz --genome genome.fai --dim metric --schema schema.tsv

Tracks without --schema (S sources, V selected BED value columns):
  BED3            one bool track, true where an interval covers the base. Needs --track,
                  and --dim for several sources.
  S = 1, V = 1    one track (position). Needs --track when the file has no header.
  S = 1, V > 1    one track (position, V). The header names are the column labels.
                  Needs --track and --dim.
  S > 1, V = 1    one track (position, S). The source labels are the column labels.
                  Needs --dim, and --track when the files have no header.
  S > 1, V > 1    one track (position, S) for each value column, with the name of
                  that column. Needs --dim.
A file without a `#chrom start end ...` header can have one value column only.
--dim with one source and one value column also makes a (position, S) track.

Bases that no interval covers are missing by default: they hold the null of the
dtype (NaN for a float, the type maximum for an integer), which the track declares
as its _FillValue. With this fill, inference keeps the type maximum free, and a
value equal to it is an error. A bool column and a BED3 mask hold false there.
Give --fill 0 when the gaps mean 0, as in a bedGraph that leaves out zero regions.

Schema rows are BED_COLUMN[<TAB>TRACK[<TAB>DTYPE[<TAB>FILL]]]. An empty or absent
TRACK takes the header name, an empty or absent DTYPE is inferred, and an empty
or absent FILL takes --fill, else the default.
